description: Team Darkrai is driven by curiosity, creativity, and a determination to explore the unknown. At NASA Space Apps, we’re combining our skills to tackle challenges on Earth and beyond, turning bold ideas into practical solutions. We’re here to learn, build, and discover what we can achieve together—with teamwork and a sense of adventure guiding us.
summary:
Lunario is a lunar south-pole landing navigator built for the NASA Space Apps Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge. A user picks a site and a stay. Lunario places the Sun and Earth, from JPL Horizons, against a local horizon traced from NASA LOLA terrain, then shows sunlight, Earth view, and a simple energy check beside the same stay on a smooth Moon.

The demonstration is one 14-day stay with fixed hardware. At Connecting Ridge, arrival on 29 June 2027 is sunlit 97.6% of the time. A smooth Moon would have left that stay dark. Arrival on 13 July 2027 drops sunlight to 16.1%, with a 211-hour dark gap, and the energy check fails. Keeping those dates and changing only the site to the de Gerlache–Shackleton ridge restores sunlight to 95.5%.

A slipped date can change which site still has power and a view of Earth. Lunario is for screening and teaching.
details:
Lunario helps you compare landing sites and dates at the Moon's south pole. Pick one of the prepared sites or type in your own coordinates, then set an arrival time (UTC) and how long you're staying. The app takes hourly Sun and Earth positions from a bundled JPL Horizons catalog and checks them against a horizon traced from LOLA elevation data. It then shows sunlight, Earth view and the longest gap in each on a timeline, a horizon chart and a south-pole map. Every terrain result sits next to a smooth-Moon version, so you can see exactly when a ridge adds or takes away sunlight. The same scenario runs in three modes. Public shows the comparison, Educator turns it into a predict-and-check lesson, and Planner exposes the solar array, power load, battery and antenna assumptions.

It's built for one question: what happens if the landing slips? Our demo keeps the hardware and the 336-hour stay the same throughout. At Connecting Ridge (89.53432°S, 209.94767°E), from 29 June 2027 11:00 UTC to 13 July 2027 11:00 UTC, 97.6% of the samples are in sunlight. On a smooth Moon the same stay gets 0%. The longest dark spell is 8 hours, the battery never drops below 7,382 Wh, and the arrays generate 432.4 kWh. Move only the arrival to 13 July 2027 and sunlight falls to 16.1%. A 211-hour dark gap opens and the energy check fails, about 52.10 kWh short. Keep that date but change only the site to the de Gerlache–Shackleton ridge (89.495°S, 222.5°E), and sunlight comes back to 95.5%, so the energy check passes again. Hours with both the Sun and Earth up go from 143 to 0 to 153. Earth contact on its own stays around 45–50% in every case, so that figure alone won't pick a site for you.

The catalog runs from 1 January 2026 up to (but not including) 1 January 2028, one sample an hour, giving 17,521 samples from Horizons DE441. We checked local azimuth and elevation against Horizons observer tables. The biggest differences were 0.00071° in Sun elevation and 0.00548° in Earth azimuth. Named horizons use the 40 m LOLA product south of 80°S, falling back to 240 m where needed. They're sampled every 1° of azimuth at observer heights of 0 m, 2 m and 10 m. Nine south-polar sites have prepared horizons. The global map also shows 40 past and planned landings, including all six Apollo missions. Where we don't have local terrain, as at Apollo 11, the app says the result is unknown rather than showing zero.

The payoff is a decision a team can see on one screen: same vehicle, one changed date, then one changed site. We want to make early screening faster, and to show clearly why average polar illumination isn't enough once a launch date moves.

The workbench is written in TypeScript and React on Next.js, with Three.js rendering the Moon, the terrain and the view of Earth. We prepared the science catalog in Python from Horizons and LOLA. The public site is static HTML and CSS on GitHub Pages, with the offline workbench embedded, so judges can open it without installing Node. Earth-orbit markers come from satellite.js and dated CelesTrak elements, including Starcloud-1. They're there for context only and don't affect the landing result.

Weather over Goldstone, Madrid and Canberra comes from Open-Meteo's 7-day hourly forecast of temperature, wind, rain and cloud. The station positions are the representative 70 m antennas listed in JPL DSN document 810-005, module 301, revision O. Each forecast is labelled with when it was fetched. It's never applied to a 2027 stay, and cloud cover isn't treated as signal loss.

We treated a launch slip as the core question, kept the hardware identical across all three cases, and showed the smooth-Moon comparison so you can see the terrain doing the work. We also kept the verdict at "conditional" on purpose. Hourly samples mean sunrise is a range rather than an exact time. The 40 m grid smooths out sharp ridges. The lander is generic. And "Earth above the hills" is a geometry check, not a booked slot on the Deep Space Network.
